pearls: Case management pays off most for chronic, complex, recurrent, multi-service problems; a short, self-limited illness rarely needs it.
The case manager should be involved from admission, not the day of discharge.
A change in clinical condition or in discharge/transfer plans is an automatic trigger to revise the plan.
For a pathway variance, the bedside nurse assesses, keeps the client safe, follows the pathway’s notification instructions, and initiates prescribed next steps.
Group variance trends point to system problems; the case manager analyzes them and feeds the quality management system.
Holistic assessment includes caregivers, home layout, equipment, finances, culture, religion, and complementary therapies.
End-of-life case management includes honest talks about hospice, palliative care, advance directives, and power of attorney, and honoring a wish to die at home when possible.
redFlags: A client whose function declines during the stay (can no longer transfer, new confusion): the discharge destination may no longer be safe.
A caregiver who suddenly becomes unavailable or a home that is unsafe: the discharge plan must be revised before the client leaves.
An at-risk pregnant client who discloses an abusive relationship: assess immediate safety privately before any other teaching.
Polypharmacy with several prescribers and duplicate or counteracting drugs: reconcile before discharge.
A pattern of the same variance across several clients: a system problem that needs quality review, not just individual fixes.
recap: Case management coordinates health and social services over time for individuals with complex needs; goals include better experience, lower cost, more choices, and better population health.
Settings: PCMH/provider-based, hospital-based (discharge planners), and community, insurer, or employer-based.
Four responsibilities: holistic assessment, culturally aligned planning, interprofessional coordination, and monitoring with revision.
High-risk triggers: high-risk DRGs, comorbidities, stays of 3 days or more, ventilator or home-health needs, functional decline.
Five essential elements: qualified case manager from admission, dedicated team, organizational support, quality management system, critical pathways.
Pathway components: diagnosis, interdisciplinary interventions, time frames, expected outcomes.
Variances: bedside nurse notifies and initiates next steps; case manager documents, individualizes, and analyzes group trends.
Lifespan interventions are tailored to pregnant women, children with disabilities, people with behavioral or intellectual disabilities, and older adults at end of life.

checks.q: A client with Parkinson disease admitted for a urinary tract infection was walking independently on admission; on day 4 the client needs two-person assistance to transfer. Discharge home with the spouse is planned for tomorrow. What should the nurse and case manager do?
checks.a: Treat this as a red flag: reassess function, notify the provider and case manager, involve PT/OT and the family, and revise the discharge plan (home health vs. rehabilitation facility) before discharge.

checks.q: Over 2 months, the case manager notes that most clients on the colectomy pathway miss the day-2 ambulation goal on weekends only. What does this suggest, and what is the best response?
checks.a: A system-related variance (for example, reduced weekend PT staffing). The case manager should analyze the trend and refer it for quality review rather than adjusting each client’s pathway separately.

checks.q: A 15-year-old who is 18 weeks pregnant has had no prenatal care and lives with an older boyfriend who controls her phone. What should the maternity case manager address first?
checks.a: Her immediate safety: speak with her privately and assess for abuse and danger. Then arrange prenatal care (which she can consent to herself under NC law) and make the required reports: in NC, suspected abuse or neglect involving a parent or caretaker goes to the county DSS (G.S. 7B-301), and a suspected sexual offense against a juvenile must also be reported to law enforcement (G.S. 14-318.6). Follow agency policy, involve the team, and report suspicion without waiting for proof.

checks.q: A client with terminal cancer sees an oncologist, a cardiologist, and a pain specialist and has three prescriptions for opioid or sedating drugs. What case management action is the priority?
checks.a: Reconcile medications with the team to eliminate duplication and counteracting or dangerous combinations, then align care with the client’s goals (for example, palliative or hospice care).

checks.q: A family asks why their child with a repaired cleft palate still has a case manager. What explanation fits?
checks.a: Correctable conditions still need coordinated surgery stages, feeding and speech therapy, counseling, and follow-up; the case manager links these services until goals are met.

checks.q: A new nurse says, “The critical pathway is the order set, so I must follow it exactly no matter what.” How should the preceptor correct this?
checks.a: Pathways are standardized guides for predictable conditions; they are individualized for comorbidities, and deviations (variances) must be recognized, reported per the pathway, and addressed, not ignored or forced.

topics.title: Exemplar 39.B: Cost-Effective Care, Payment Sources & Health Systems
topics.summary: Cost-effective care delivers the best outcome for the resources used; nurses contribute by preventing complications and readmissions, avoiding waste and duplication, helping clients understand and navigate their coverage, and advocating for access, without ever trading away safety.
objectives: Explain the U.S. healthcare cost paradox and the main drivers of high U.S. costs.
Distinguish public insurance, private insurance, and out-of-pocket payment, and compare Medicare with Medicaid.
Apply cost-sharing terms (premium, deductible, co-payment, coinsurance, out-of-network penalty) to a client’s question or bill.
Explain how DRGs and the prospective payment system create incentives around length of stay, complications, and readmissions.
Compare the four international health-system categories: socialized medicine, socialized insurance, mandatory health insurance, and voluntary insurance.
Select nursing actions that reduce cost while maintaining or improving safety and quality, and recognize cost-saving shortcuts that are unsafe.
topics.bigPicture:
Healthcare costs are not just an administrator’s problem. When a client develops a catheter-associated urinary tract infection, falls and breaks a hip, or is readmitted 5 days after discharge because nobody confirmed they could afford their inhaler, the cost is human first and financial second. Cost-effective care means getting the best possible outcome for the money and effort spent. Almost every cost-effective action a nurse takes is also a safety action: preventing complications, avoiding duplicate tests, teaching well enough to prevent readmission, and linking clients to resources they can actually use.

The United States spends more on healthcare than any other country, yet compared with other high-income countries it has the highest obesity rate, the highest chronic disease burden, the highest suicide rate, and the lowest life expectancy. Understanding why (administrative waste, high drug prices, public health shocks) and how care is paid for (public insurance, private insurance, and out-of-pocket payment) helps you answer the client who asks, “Why do I owe this?” or says, “I can’t afford that prescription.”

On the NCLEX, cost questions are usually disguised as teaching (explain a deductible or the difference between Medicare and Medicaid), advocacy (help a client who cannot afford care), safety (reject a cost-saving shortcut that harms clients), or prioritization (which action prevents an expensive complication). The rule that wins nearly every time: cost savings never justify compromising safety, scope, or the standard of care.

keyTerms.def: Care that achieves the best outcome for the resources used by preventing complications, eliminating waste and duplication, and matching services to need without compromising safety or quality.
Government-funded payment for healthcare for people who meet eligibility criteria; key U.S. examples are Medicare and Medicaid (also CHIP).
Coverage provided by private or publicly owned companies, often employer-sponsored or individually purchased; examples include Blue Cross Blue Shield, Kaiser Permanente, and Aetna.
Money the client pays directly for care, including self-pay for the uninsured and cost sharing for the insured.

Federal health insurance for people 65 and older and for some younger people with qualifying disabilities, end-stage renal disease, or ALS; Part A covers hospital care, Part B outpatient and provider services, Part C is Medicare Advantage, and Part D covers prescription drugs.

Joint federal–state public insurance for eligible people with low income, including children, pregnant people, people with disabilities, and many older adults needing long-term care; eligibility and benefits vary by state.
The regular (often monthly) amount paid to keep insurance coverage active, whether or not care is used.
The fixed annual amount the client must pay before insurance begins to cover costs.
A fixed fee the client pays for selected services or prescriptions (for example, $30 per office visit).
The client’s percentage share of the cost of a covered service after the deductible is met (for example, 20%).
Higher out-of-pocket costs incurred when care is received outside the plan’s approved network or without meeting coverage criteria.
Standardized classifications of diagnoses (and procedures) used to set a predetermined payment for a hospital stay.

A payment method in which the payer (for example, Medicare) sets the payment in advance based on the DRG rather than on the hospital’s actual costs; if care costs less the hospital keeps the difference, and if it costs more the hospital absorbs the loss.
A measure of disease burden combining years of life lost to premature death and years lived with disability; the U.S. DALY rate in 2017 was 31% higher than in comparable developed countries.

A system in which the state owns and controls healthcare services and physicians are government employees who derive virtually all income from the government (for example, United Kingdom, Sweden, Denmark).

A system in which the government covers all medically necessary services (physician, hospital, and other benefits) through universal public insurance while delivery may remain private or independent (for example, Canada).

A system in which law requires employers and employees to contribute to insurance funds (often nonprofit “sickness funds”) that cover nearly everyone, with mostly private delivery (for example, Germany, France, Japan).
A system in which purchasing insurance is largely voluntary, through employers or individuals, with public programs for specific groups; the United States is the main example.
Delivery of health services and monitoring at a distance using technology; a cost-containment and access strategy, especially for rural and chronically ill clients.

sections.heading: The U.S. paradox: highest spending, weaker outcomes
sections.body:
According to The Commonwealth Fund, the U.S. spends more on healthcare than any other high-income country, yet it has the highest obesity rate, the highest chronic disease burden, the highest suicide rate, and the lowest life expectancy among those peers. In 2017 the U.S. DALY rate (a combined measure of early death and disability) was 31% higher than in other developed countries. Unlike Canada and the United Kingdom, the U.S. does not have a nationalized or socialized system.

Why so expensive? The major drivers are administrative waste (billing complexity, many payers with different rules), high pharmaceutical prices, and public health shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic, estimated at more than $16 trillion in costs across the U.S. economy. Proposed and current cost-containment and access strategies include expanding telehealth, improving price transparency, continuous quality monitoring, allowing small businesses to pool for insurance, expanding cross-state insurance purchasing, and exploring Medicare-for-All or public insurance options.

The nursing takeaway: spending more does not automatically produce health. Prevention, chronic disease management, and coordinated care are where nurses move both outcomes and cost.
bullets: Spending is highest, but outcomes lag: obesity, chronic disease, suicide, life expectancy.
Drivers: administrative waste, drug prices, public health shocks (COVID-19, more than $16 trillion).
Strategies: telehealth, transparency, quality monitoring, small-business pooling, cross-state purchasing, public-option or Medicare-for-All proposals.

check.q: A community member says, “Because America spends the most, we must have the healthiest people.” How should the nurse respond?
check.a: Explain that U.S. spending is highest but outcomes trail other high-income countries (shorter life expectancy, higher chronic disease burden), largely due to administrative costs, drug prices, and gaps in prevention and access.

sections.heading: Three ways care is paid for
sections.body:
Every bill is paid through one of three channels, or a combination. Public insurance is government-funded for people who meet eligibility criteria, chiefly Medicare and Medicaid (and the Children’s Health Insurance Program). Private insurance is sold by companies such as Blue Cross Blue Shield, Kaiser Permanente, and Aetna, usually through an employer or bought individually. Direct out-of-pocket (OOP) payment is what the client pays personally, either as a self-pay (uninsured) client or as cost sharing within a plan.

The nurse does not decide coverage, but payer source shapes the plan: which rehabilitation facility will accept the client, whether a medication is on the formulary, and how many home-health visits are authorized. That is why the case manager and social worker need early, accurate information, and why the nurse should ask about cost barriers instead of assuming adherence.

sections.heading: Medicare vs. Medicaid: the comparison clients get wrong
sections.body:
These two programs have similar names and opposite logic. Medicare is federal and based mainly on age (65 and older) or certain disabilities and conditions (qualifying long-term disability, end-stage renal disease, ALS); income does not determine eligibility. Medicaid is a joint federal–state program based mainly on income and need; eligibility and benefits vary by state. A person can qualify for both (“dual eligible”).

A frequent exam trap involves long-term care. Medicare covers short-term skilled nursing or rehabilitation after a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and home health when criteria are met, but it does not pay for long-term custodial care (help with bathing and dressing in a nursing home indefinitely). Medicaid is the major public payer for long-term nursing-home care for people who meet its financial criteria.

check.a: Medicare eligibility is based on age (65 and older) or qualifying disability, not income; savings affect Medicaid eligibility, not Medicare.

sections.heading: Cost-sharing vocabulary: premium, deductible, co-pay, coinsurance, out-of-network
sections.body:
Clients are often surprised by bills because these terms sound alike. The premium keeps coverage active. The yearly deductible is the amount the client pays first, each year, before the plan starts paying. A co-payment is a fixed dollar fee for a specific service or prescription. Coinsurance is a percentage the client pays after the deductible. An out-of-network or nonparticipating penalty means higher OOP cost when care is received outside the network or without meeting coverage criteria (for example, no referral in an HMO or no prior authorization).

Being able to walk a client through these terms is client teaching and advocacy. It also prevents a common safety problem: clients who skip care because they misunderstand what they owe.

Of the remaining $2,000, the client pays 20%, or $400. Total client cost: $1,400; the plan pays $1,600. If the client later has a $30 co-pay office visit, the co-pay is owed in addition.

check.q: A client says, “I pay my premium every month, so my MRI should be free.” What is the best explanation?
check.a: The premium keeps the coverage active, but most plans require the client to meet the yearly deductible (and then any coinsurance or co-pay) before the plan pays its share.

sections.heading: DRGs and prospective payment: why length of stay and complications matter
sections.body:
Under a prospective payment system (PPS), Medicare and many other payers decide in advance how much they will pay for a hospital stay, based on the client’s DRG. The payment does not rise because the client stays longer or needs more supplies. If the hospital provides safe care for less than the payment, it keeps the difference; if the stay costs more, the hospital absorbs the loss.

This creates two incentives. The good one: hospitals work hard to prevent complications, coordinate care, and discharge on time. The risky one: pressure for early discharge, which can increase readmissions if clients go home before they are ready or without adequate teaching. Payers have responded: Medicare does not pay hospitals extra for certain preventable hospital-acquired conditions (for example, stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, falls with injury, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, and central line–associated bloodstream infections), and it penalizes hospitals with excess 30-day readmissions for selected conditions. In other words, the payment system now rewards exactly what good nursing does: prevent harm and prepare clients for discharge.
sections.analogy: PPS is like a fixed-price catering contract. The caterer is paid a set price per guest no matter how much food is used. A smart caterer avoids waste; a careless one runs out of food and the guests go home hungry and come back angry. The best result is enough of the right food for each guest, with nothing thrown away.
sections.example: A client admitted for a hip fracture repair develops a stage 3 pressure injury on day 4 because repositioning was missed. The stay lengthens by 6 days and requires wound care and a specialty mattress. Under PPS, the hospital receives essentially the same payment as if the injury had not happened, so it absorbs the extra cost, and the client suffers pain, delayed rehabilitation, and infection risk. Repositioning every 2 hours, a skin assessment each shift, and nutrition support would have cost far less.

check.q: Under a prospective payment system, a client admitted for pneumonia develops a catheter-associated urinary tract infection that adds 3 days to the stay. Who bears most of the cost of the extra days, and what is the nursing lesson?
check.a: The hospital. The payment was set in advance by the DRG, and Medicare does not pay extra for this hospital-acquired condition. The nursing lesson is that prevention (insert catheters only when indicated, maintain them correctly, and remove them as soon as they are no longer needed) is both safe care and cost-effective care.

sections.heading: Four international health-system categories
sections.body:
Countries organize health financing in four broad ways. Two are described on p. 2630 of the source (socialized medicine and socialized insurance), and two more (mandatory health insurance and voluntary insurance) complete the classic framework. The key distinction is who owns the delivery system and who pays.

In socialized medicine, the government both pays and owns: hospitals are state-owned, and physicians are government employees (United Kingdom, Sweden, Denmark). In socialized insurance, the government pays for all medically necessary services through universal public insurance, but providers are largely private or independent (Canada). In mandatory health insurance, the law requires employers and employees to contribute to insurance funds that cover nearly everyone, with mostly private delivery (Germany, France, Japan). In voluntary insurance, buying insurance is mostly a choice through employers or individuals, with public programs for specific groups (the United States).

check.a: Socialized insurance: the government pays for medically necessary care, but delivery is private. It differs from socialized medicine, in which the state owns facilities and employs physicians.

sections.heading: The bedside nurse’s role in cost-effective care
sections.body:
Nurses influence a large share of hospital costs through the care they give every hour. The highest-value nursing actions are the ones that prevent expensive harm and duplication while improving the client’s experience. They fall into a few groups: prevent complications (fall, pressure-injury, VTE, and infection bundles; removing urinary catheters as soon as they are no longer indicated), avoid duplication and waste (check existing results before requesting tests, cluster care and lab draws, use supplies appropriately), prepare clients for discharge (teach-back, medication affordability checks, follow-up appointments, home-health referrals) to prevent readmissions, use telehealth and community resources for monitoring and follow-up, and advocate for clients facing cost barriers (social work, case management, medication assistance, generic alternatives discussed with the provider).

Just as important is knowing what not to do. Reusing single-use items, skipping reassessments, delegating RN work to UAP to save salary, or choosing a cheaper product that is contraindicated for the client are not cost-effective; they shift cost into harm, liability, and readmission.
bullets: Prevent: falls, pressure injuries, CAUTI, CLABSI, VTE, aspiration.
Avoid duplication: check for existing labs and imaging; coordinate scheduling.
Prepare for discharge: teach-back, affordability check, follow-up within days, home-health or telehealth monitoring.
Advocate: refer to social work or case management; ask the provider about lower-cost equivalent therapy.
Never: reuse single-use devices, skip assessments, delegate outside scope, or substitute a contraindicated product.
sections.example: During discharge teaching, a client with COPD says the new inhaler costs $350 a month and asks whether it is “really necessary.” The nurse does not tell the client to skip it or to use it every other day. The nurse asks about coverage and resources, notifies the provider about the cost barrier so a covered or lower-cost equivalent can be considered, and refers the client to social work for medication assistance before discharge. Preventing one COPD exacerbation admission saves far more than the cost of the intervention.

check.q: To save money, a coworker suggests reusing a single-use suction catheter on the same client for the whole shift. How should the nurse respond?
check.a: Decline. Reusing single-use devices increases infection risk and violates the standard of care, and one infection would cost far more than the catheter. Suggest legitimate savings instead, such as checking for duplicate lab orders, clustering care, or reviewing supply use with the unit council.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: cost-effective care and coverage questions
sections.body: Common patterns: (1) Client teaching on coverage terms or Medicare vs. Medicaid, often as “which statement indicates a need for further teaching?” (2) Cost barrier: a client cannot afford a medication or follow-up; the best answer assesses the barrier, involves the provider, and refers to social work or case management, never advises skipping or rationing therapy on the nurse’s own authority. (3) Cost vs. safety: a manager or coworker proposes a shortcut; the best answer protects safety and scope while offering a legitimate efficiency. (4) Payment incentives: why preventing a hospital-acquired condition or readmission matters under PPS.
steps: Read the stem: “A client being discharged after a heart failure exacerbation says, ‘I can’t afford all of these pills, so I’ll take the water pill every other day.’ What is the nurse’s best response? (A) ‘Taking it every other day is fine as long as you weigh yourself.’ (B) ‘Let’s look at what each medicine costs you. I’ll let your provider know, and I’ll ask the social worker about help paying for them.’ (C) ‘You must take every medication exactly as prescribed or you will be readmitted.’ (D) ‘Ask your pharmacist which pills you can safely stop.’”
Identify what is being asked: the best response to a cost barrier that is causing unsafe nonadherence.
Spot cues: heart failure (diuretic omission risks fluid overload and readmission), the client volunteers a cost problem, the client is planning a self-made change.

Eliminate: (A) endorses an unsafe dose change outside the nurse’s scope. (C) is true-ish but threatening and leaves the barrier unsolved. (D) shifts responsibility and implies stopping medications without the prescriber.

Choose (B): it assesses the barrier, communicates with the prescriber, and mobilizes resources. Reusable strategy: when cost is the problem, the answer is assess, communicate, refer, and never reduce therapy without the prescriber.

sections.heading: Worked case: the budget meeting
sections.body: You are the charge nurse on a 24-bed medical-surgical unit. The finance office reports that the unit’s average length of stay is above the DRG benchmark, supply costs are up, and the unit had 4 catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) and 3 falls with injury last quarter. 30-day readmissions for clients with heart failure are 24%. A manager proposes replacing two RN positions with UAP and “buying the cheaper skin barrier.” You are asked to propose a plan.
steps: Recognize cues: preventable hospital-acquired conditions (CAUTI, falls with injury) lengthen stays and are not paid extra under PPS; readmissions carry penalties; the proposed staffing cut reduces RN hours on a unit with acuity problems.

Analyze: the biggest costs come from complications and readmissions, not from RN salaries. Evidence links RN staffing and education to lower mortality and fewer adverse events, so cutting RNs is likely to increase cost.

Generate solutions: implement a nurse-driven catheter removal protocol and daily necessity review; strengthen the fall bundle (hourly rounding, toileting schedule, bed alarms for high-risk clients); a heart-failure discharge bundle with teach-back, affordability checks, follow-up within 7 days, and telehealth weight monitoring; review supply use with the wound-care nurse (a lower-cost barrier is acceptable only if it is equally effective and not contraindicated).
Take action: present the data and plan to the manager, using shared-governance structures (unit practice council) so bedside nurses help design the changes.
Evaluate outcomes: track CAUTI and fall rates, length of stay, readmissions, supply costs, and client satisfaction monthly; adjust based on results.

check.q: The manager asks, “Why not just replace RNs with UAP? It saves salary.” What is the strongest evidence-based reply?
check.a: Nurse staffing and RN qualifications are linked to morbidity, mortality, and cost; fewer RN hours increases missed assessments, falls, and complications, which raise length of stay and unreimbursed costs. Match skill mix to acuity and target the complications driving cost.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body: Cost pressure does not change the law that defines who may do what. In North Carolina:
bullets: The NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and NCBON rules (21 NCAC 36 .0224 for RNs, .0225 for LPNs) keep assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment as RN responsibilities, whatever the budget.

Nurse Aide I (registry kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation) and Nurse Aide II (registry kept by NCBON; must also be on the NA I registry) may perform only tasks on their approved lists, and only when the RN decides delegation is appropriate for the specific client. Replacing licensed staff with aides cannot expand those lists.

If a client who is a disabled adult appears to be neglected or financially exploited (for example, a caregiver withholding money for medications), G.S. 108A-102 requires any person with reasonable cause to believe the adult needs protective services to report to the county DSS director; good-faith reporters are immune.

End-of-life cost conversations must center on the client’s wishes, not on cost. NC tools for documenting those wishes include the Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3), the Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (G.S. 90-321), and the MOST form.

sections.body:
Source: Module 39 study guide, Exemplar 39.B Cost-Effective Care, p. 2630 (glossary entries for public insurance, private insurance, socialized medicine, and socialized insurance; U.S. cost crisis; payment sources and cost-sharing terms; international perspectives), with the source’s note that DRGs, PPS, mandatory health insurance, and voluntary insurance continue on pp. 2631–2632. DRGs are also introduced on p. 2627.

Clarifications and additions:
bullets: The Commonwealth Fund comparisons (highest obesity, chronic disease burden, and suicide rate; lowest life expectancy) are among high-income peer countries, not all countries worldwide.

The source’s two definitions of socialized insurance (“delivery may remain private” and “universal public insurance”) are combined here: the government pays for all medically necessary services while providers remain largely private (Canada is the standard example).

Added mandatory health insurance and voluntary insurance (pp. 2631–2632 per the source) with standard examples (Germany, France, Japan; United States), plus a PPS definition, to complete the four-category framework.

Added coinsurance and premium, Medicare parts, Medicaid long-term care coverage, and CMS hospital-acquired condition and readmission payment policies, because NCLEX coverage and cost items commonly rely on them.
The app uses “client” in place of the source’s “patient.”

mnemonics.text: Co-pay = fixed dollars per service; coinsurance = percent after the deductible.

pearls: The most cost-effective nursing actions are safety actions: preventing falls, pressure injuries, infections, and readmissions.
Under PPS the hospital is paid a set amount per DRG; complications and extra days are mostly unreimbursed costs.
When a client cannot afford therapy, assess the barrier, inform the prescriber, and refer; never advise reducing or stopping medication on your own.
Medicare eligibility is age or qualifying disability, not income; Medicaid is income-based and covers long-term custodial care for those who qualify.
A deductible is paid first; a co-pay is a fixed fee; coinsurance is a percentage after the deductible.
Socialized medicine (UK) means the state owns and employs; socialized insurance (Canada) means the state pays but providers are private.
Telehealth is both a cost-containment and an access strategy, especially for rural and chronically ill clients.
redFlags: A client planning to skip, split, or space out a critical medication because of cost.
A cost-saving proposal that reuses single-use devices, skips reassessment, or delegates RN functions to UAP.
Early discharge without teach-back, follow-up, or confirmed ability to obtain medications and equipment: high readmission risk.
A client who avoids needed care because of a misunderstood bill or fear of cost.
Rising hospital-acquired conditions on a unit: a quality and cost problem that needs immediate prevention bundles.
recap: The U.S. spends the most among high-income countries yet has worse outcomes; drivers include administrative waste, drug prices, and public health shocks.
Payment comes from public insurance (Medicare, Medicaid), private insurance (BCBS, Kaiser, Aetna), or out-of-pocket.
Medicare: federal, age 65+ or disability; Medicaid: federal–state, income-based, long-term care.
Premium keeps coverage; deductible comes first; co-pay is fixed; coinsurance is a percentage; out-of-network costs more.
DRGs classify stays; PPS pays a fixed amount in advance, rewarding prevention of complications and readmissions.
Four systems: socialized medicine, socialized insurance, mandatory health insurance, voluntary insurance.
Nurses contain cost by preventing harm, avoiding duplication, preparing clients for discharge, using telehealth, and advocating.
Cost savings never justify compromising safety, scope, or the standard of care.

checks.q: A client has met a $500 deductible and has 20% coinsurance. A covered emergency visit costs $1,200. How much does the client owe, and why?
checks.a: $240. The deductible is already met, so the client pays the 20% coinsurance share of $1,200.

checks.q: A nurse suggests leaving urinary catheters in place until discharge “to save nursing time.” Why is this not cost-effective?
checks.a: Catheters left in place increase CAUTI risk; CAUTI lengthens stays, harms clients, and is a hospital-acquired condition that Medicare does not pay extra for. Removing catheters when no longer indicated is safer and cheaper.

checks.q: A client from the United Kingdom asks why U.S. hospitals ask about insurance at registration. What is the key difference to explain?
checks.a: The UK uses socialized medicine (the government owns facilities and pays providers), while the U.S. relies largely on voluntary insurance plus public programs for eligible groups, so payer source must be identified.

checks.q: A 45-year-old with no disability, a low income, and two children asks whether Medicare will cover a hospital stay. What is the most accurate response?
checks.a: Medicare is generally for people 65 and older or with qualifying disabilities; based on income and family status, the client may qualify for Medicaid, and the social worker or financial counselor can help apply.

checks.q: A client’s DRG payment is fixed, and the client is ready for discharge on day 3, but has not demonstrated how to use a new inhaler. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Complete teaching with teach-back (and arrange follow-up) before discharge; inadequate teaching risks readmission, which costs more and harms the client.

checks.q: A rural client with heart failure misses follow-up visits because the clinic is 70 miles away. Which cost-effective strategy also improves access?
checks.a: Telehealth follow-up with remote weight and symptom monitoring, coordinated by the case manager or clinic.
